nsupdate-add-a.bin is a real RFC 2136 update captured off the wire, kept so
the TSIG computation in this package can be checked against an implementation
nobody here wrote.

How it was made
---------------

A throwaway UDP listener bound to 127.0.0.1:5399 and wrote the first datagram
it received to the file. Then, on the same machine (macOS, ISC nsupdate
9.10.6 at /usr/bin/nsupdate):

    nsupdate -y hmac-sha256:ddns-key:Y29yZWRoY3AtZGRucy1nb2xkZW4tdGVzdC1rZXkhISE= <<'CMDS'
    server 127.0.0.1 5399
    zone home.lan
    update add host.home.lan 300 A 10.0.0.5
    send
    CMDS

The listener never answered, so nsupdate retried and gave up. Only the first
datagram was kept.

What is in it
-------------

    key name        ddns-key.
    algorithm       hmac-sha256.
    secret          Y29yZWRoY3AtZGRucy1nb2xkZW4tdGVzdC1rZXkhISE=
                    ("coredhcp-ddns-golden-test-key!!!", 32 octets)
    message ID      0xe06e
    time signed     1788589641 (2026-09-05T06:27:21Z)
    fudge           300
    MAC             e3500ee31020867d470b67d236f7151f94ee8c0b78df905892de2905378c5cc2
    TSIG record at  offset 47
    total length    128 octets

The secret is a test key and nothing else has ever used it.

One difference from what this package sends
-------------------------------------------

nsupdate compresses names: the update record's owner reads as "host" followed
by a pointer to home.lan. in the zone section. This package writes every name
out in full, so the two messages are not byte for byte comparable and the
golden file is used for the MAC only. That is the interesting half anyway: the
MAC covers the message exactly as it was rendered, so recomputing it over the
captured bytes checks the digest, the TSIG variables and the field layout
without depending on how the names were packed.
